entities.name: François Gédéon Bailly de Monthion
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
François Gédéon, comte Bailly de Monthion (1776–1850), emerged as a pivotal figure in the French military apparatus during the tumultuous Napoleonic Wars and the subsequent Bourbon Restoration. Born in Saint-Denis, Île-de-France, he rose through the ranks from a humble volunteer in 1792 to a respected general, primarily distinguishing himself as an exceptionally capable chief of staff and aide-de-camp. His career trajectory mirrored the meritocratic ideals of the French Revolution, allowing a talented individual to achieve high command and exert significant influence over the strategic and logistical execution of Napoleon Bonaparte's most celebrated campaigns across Europe.

Bailly de Monthion's operational career began in the Army of the Rhine and Moselle, where his administrative talents were quickly recognized. He became aide-de-camp to General Louis Baraguey d'Hilliers in 1800, and by 1805, he was serving as Chief of Staff to Marshal Louis-Alexandre Berthier, Napoleon's indispensable Major General, playing a crucial role in the Austerlitz campaign. His meticulous organizational skills and strategic acumen were further tested and proven in the Jena-Auerstedt (1806), Eylau (1807), and Wagram (1809) campaigns. Elevated to Général de Brigade in 1811, he participated in the disastrous Russian Campaign of 1812 and the subsequent German campaign of 1813, including the Battle of Leipzig, before being promoted to Général de Division during the final defense of France in 1814. He notably served as Napoleon's chief of staff during the Hundred Days, including the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: François Gédéon Bailly de Monthion was a critical, if often unsung, figure in the operational success of Napoleon's Grande Armée, contributing significantly to key campaigns like Austerlitz and Wagram through his staff work. His ability to adapt and serve through the Restoration also provided crucial continuity for the French military.
